content: The symptoms of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus (MERS-CoV) infection typically include fever, cough, shortness of breath, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea and vomiting. MERS-CoV infection should be suspected in individuals presenting with a fever of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, along with pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome, as confirmed by clinical or radiological evidence. This suspicion is heightened if the individual has one of the following risk factors: 1. A history of travel to countries located in or near the Arabian Peninsula within 14 days prior to the onset of symptoms. 2. Close contact with a symptomatic traveler who developed fever and acute respiratory illness (not necessarily pneumonia) within 14 days after traveling from countries in or near the Arabian Peninsula. 3. Membership in a cluster of patients with severe acute respiratory illness (e.g., fever and pneumonia requiring hospitalization) of unknown cause, where MERS-CoV is being investigated in collaboration with state and local health authorities. The most common symptoms reported in MERS-CoV cases include fever (98%), cough (83%), and shortness of breath (72%). Gastrointestinal symptoms are also observed, with diarrhea occurring in 26% of cases and vomiting in 21%. Nearly all patients (96%) diagnosed with MERS-CoV infection have at least one chronic medical condition. The most frequently reported comorbidities include diabetes (68%), hypertension (34%), heart disease (28%), and kidney disease (49%). Additionally, 72% of patients have more than one chronic condition. In a retrospective study involving 47 patients with confirmed MERS-CoV infection, 89% (42 patients) required intensive care, and 72% (34 patients) needed mechanical ventilation.
